> 姤。女壯，勿用取女。

Hexagram 44 is about an encounter that was not sought, and its character is built with a sound that carries meaning.

## 姤 is 從女，后聲

姤: 女 as the semantic side, 后 as the sound — and 后 is not only the sound. 爾雅·釋詁: 后，君也.

One woman behind the many: the latecomer, the one who arrives afterward — the one who came without being called.

The 彖 and 序卦 both gloss it directly: 姤，遇也. And the book uses that and nothing else.

But 遇 in pre-Qin usage is not as light as "to meet." In the 易 it carries 不期 — not expected, not summoned. It came by itself.

Which is why it is hard to refuse: it does not knock.

## 女壯: 壯 means momentum, not muscle

壯 in pre-Qin means the force of a thing rising, not physical bulk. And the 彖 fixes it in the next clause: 不可與長也 — it cannot be given length.

So 壯 is "growing fast," not "grown large." The line is not saying the woman is strong. It is saying the arrival is quick.

## 取女: why the marriage word

取 is 娶. 取女 is taking a wife — a relation meant to last, not a single meeting.

And the judgement of a hexagram about encounters talks about marriage, because marriage is how an 遇 is turned into something 久.

Which is exactly what 姤 warns about: an encounter is permitted; length is not.

## 系于金柅

柅 is the wooden chock put under a wheel to stop a cart. Wang Bi: 金柅，制動之主 — the master of braking.

金 is not ornament, it is material: a wooden chock rots; a metal one does not break.

So the picture: the cart has just started to move, and the chock is already under the wheel.

## 羸豕孚蹢躅

羸: lean, thin. 豕: pig — and the pig in pre-Qin is an image of restlessness, of a motion that cannot be shut up.

(Another reading takes 羸 as 累, tied, which gives: the tied pig is still struggling. Both readings point at the same thing — it is held, and it has not stopped.)

蹢躅: two steps forward, one back; wanting to go and stopping.

孚: one reading is "trustworthy, genuinely so," i.e. this is simply its nature; another is 浮, restless. Wang Bi: 孚，猶務也 — it is bent on going forward.

Three characters, one exact drawing: a lean pig tied under a cart, pacing back and forth, having moved not one step, and not having stopped for a moment.

## 包: kitchen or wrapping

包 appears three times, and the readings differ.

九二 包有魚 and 九四 包無魚: most commentators read 包 as 庖, the kitchen. A fish in the kitchen is one that is here and can be managed; a kitchen without fish is one that is gone.

九五 以杞包瓜: here 包 is to wrap — willow stems wrapped around a melon.

One character, two readings, and the hexagram's imagery splits into two layers accordingly: possession below, containment above.

## 含章，有隕自天

九五: containing the pattern, and something falls from heaven.

The line does not go out and seize the arrival. It holds what is bright inside and waits — and what arrives then comes from above, not from the encounter.

Which is 姤's answer to 姤: the only safe way to receive something that arrives uninvited is to be the kind of place things fall into.

## The test

Take an opportunity that appeared without your looking for it — a person, a deal, an opening. Ask the hexagram's two questions: is this an 遇 or a 取? And is there a chock under the wheel before the cart moves?
